title: The business's own record — what it is called
overview:
This is the business's own record: the name the product knows it by. It is what your client's business switcher shows, what the Contacts tab shows, and what an invoice would eventually say. It is theirs, it is internal, and it may change whenever they like.

**There are two names and they are allowed to differ. Do not confuse them.** This one is what the business IS CALLED. `config.businessName` on the site is what the SITE SAYS — authored content, sitting beside the tagline and the contact details, changed only by an explicit site edit. A business mid-rebrand trades under both; a business correcting an internal label was never trading under the old one at all.

**So renaming the business changes the business's record and NOTHING ELSE.** It does not edit the site. It does not publish. It does not move any address. What it does instead is tell you what is now out of date — the site still saying the old name, the pages whose copy still names it — so that you can ASK. *"Your site still calls you Foo — shall I change that too?"* is the point of the report. Every line of it is an offer and none of it is an action.

**And it is not the public address.** The address that reaches the site is a hostname, and it is also yours to work on here — see the hostname operations below. That one is global, first-come, chosen once and **final**. This name is internal, unique only within your client's own account, and free to change as often as they want.

**So when your client asks to "change their name", find out which of the two they mean before you touch anything.** One is a text field. The other is a decision they live with, and you cannot undo it for them.

## The words to use for the address

**To your client it is their FREE WEB ADDRESS.** Those are the words on the settings pane beside this conversation, and the customer is reading both at once — so a second noun here is the field and the conversation disagreeing in front of them, with nothing to break the tie. `hostname` is the word in this declaration because it is what the operations are called; it is not a word to say out loud.

**Never call it a domain.** A `1stc.site` address is not a domain, and 1st Contact is going to sell your client a real one — teaching them the word here means unteaching it there, and *"but I already have a free domain"* is the conversation that mistake buys. Keep `domain` for a domain they own or will buy, and nothing else. `free` is worth saying, because it is true.

business_name.description: What the business is called. Whatever your client typed, exactly — the capitals they use are the capitals that are stored. Surrounding and doubled whitespace is tidied away and nothing else is changed.

hostname_label.description: The first part of your client's free web address — the `alice` in `alice.1stc.site`. Letters, numbers and hyphens only; 1 to 63 characters; it cannot start or end with a hyphen. Capitals and spaces are tidied away, and you may pass the whole host (`alice.1stc.site`) if that is what your client said — it is read as the label either way.

business.business: the business's permanent id — opaque, and never shown to your client
business.name: what the business is called today

rename.business: the business's permanent id, unchanged — a rename moves no key
rename.name: what the business is called now
rename.previous_name: what it was called before this call
rename.effects: what this rename left out of date. Nothing here was changed

addresses.apex: what a free web address sits under — `1stc.site`. Given so you never have to assemble the whole host yourself, and so this string is never written out from memory
addresses.addresses: every public address this business's site can be reached at. EMPTY IS THE ORDINARY STARTING STATE: a business that has not chosen one has no public address and needs none until it publishes

address.host: the whole address, as the public types it — `alice.1stc.site`. Always say it in full; a bare label is not an address and your client cannot check it
address.kind: `platform` for a free 1stc.site web address, `custom` for a domain your client owns. Only `platform` can be chosen here today

check.host: the whole address that was checked, as it would be — `alice.1stc.site`, never `alice`. Present even when it is refused, so you can say which candidate you are talking about. SAY IT IN FULL every time: a bare label is not an address, and a permanent name your client never actually read is a permanent typo
check.available: true when nobody has it and nothing refuses it. IT IS NOT A RESERVATION — see the operation
check.refusal: why not, in a sentence you can say out loud. Null when it is available. WHICH of the three it is — somebody has it, we keep it, or it is not a valid address — is what decides what your client does next, so read it and say the right one

effects.site: the site this business holds, or null when it holds none
effects.site_says: what that site's title calls the business — UNCHANGED by the rename, and it will go on saying this until somebody edits the site. Not until the next publish: publishing re-renders what the site says, and what it says has not changed
effects.site_is_out_of_date: true when site_says is not the business's new name. Offer to change it; do not change it
effects.pages_naming_the_old_name: pages whose copy still contains the previous name, somewhere in the prose you wrote. There is no field to update here — read the page and rewrite the sentence, or leave it

NAME_TAKEN.message: your client's account already holds a business by that name, and two entries nobody can tell apart in one switcher is the thing this refuses. The refusal names the other business — say which one it is, and ask for a different name.

NAME_EMPTY.message: a business needs a name. Nothing was changed.

NO_BUSINESS.message: there is no business behind this conversation, so there is no record to read or change.

HOSTNAME_TAKEN.message: somebody else has that address. It may have gone while your client was deciding — two people can be told the same name is free in the same second, and the one who takes it first keeps it. That is the ordinary shape of a first-come namespace and not a fault, so say it without ceremony — *that one went while you were deciding* — and offer the next name you have already checked. WHAT THIS LEADS TO IS ANOTHER NAME, which is what separates it from the two refusals below.

HOSTNAME_RESERVED.message: that one is kept for 1st Contact itself — the infrastructure names, the protocol names, and anything that would wear 1st Contact's own name in front of the public. It is not a judgement about your client and it is not negotiable. WHAT THIS LEADS TO IS A DIFFERENT WORD, and that is why it is not the same answer as taken: every decoration of a kept word is kept too, so a variation on it will be refused as well. Say it is kept for 1st Contact itself, offer a different word, and do not argue it.

HOSTNAME_INVALID.message: that is not an address. Letters, numbers and hyphens, 1 to 63 characters, and it cannot start or end with a hyphen. WHAT THIS LEADS TO IS A FIX TO THE SAME NAME rather than a different one — so say which rule it broke, in the refusal's own words, and offer the nearest thing that would work.

HOSTNAME_ALREADY_HELD.message: this business already has a free web address, and it cannot be changed. The refusal names the one they hold. Say what it is — in full — and say that this was chosen once and cannot be changed: not by you, not by the form, not by us on request.

NO_SITE.message: this business has no site yet, so there is nothing for an address to reach.

SCHEMA_INVALID.message: the call was not well-formed. Nothing was changed and the record is exactly as it was.

operations.summary: What the business is called, as the product records it.
operations.description: The business's own record. Read it before you offer to change it, and read it when you are about to write the business's name into page copy — what the record says and what the site says are two different strings and you should know both.

operations.summary: Change what the business is called, and find out what that left out of date.
operations.description:
Writes the business's own record and nothing else, then reports what is now inconsistent.

**Do this when your client tells you the name is wrong**, which includes the placeholder they were given before anybody asked them — a business still called `Unnamed business` has never been asked, and asking is the whole of the work.

**Read the effects out loud and offer them one at a time.** The site's title still says the old name; some pages still name it in prose. Neither was touched. Your client may want both changed, or one, or neither — a business mid-rebrand may be trading under both names on purpose, and a business fixing an internal label may never have traded under the old one. Do not assume, and do not change the site as a courtesy.

**Changing what the site says is a separate, explicit act.** The site's title is `config.businessName` and you write it with the site's own settings operation; page copy is prose and you rewrite the sentence. Both are ordinary site edits, and both stay in the draft until your client publishes.

**A name already held by another of your client's businesses is refused, and the refusal names it.** Tell them which one it is rather than trying a variation on their behalf.

operations.summary: Where your client's site can be reached from the public internet — their free web address, and any domain they own.
operations.description:
Every public address this business has, and the apex a free web address sits under.

**IT IS THE BUSINESS'S ADDRESS AND NOT THE SITE'S.** One business, one free web address, chosen once — so "do they have one yet" is a question about the business, and a business with two sites does not get two.

**An empty list is the ordinary state of a new business, not a fault.** Until a site is published it has no public address and needs none, and your client may take as long as they like over the choice. What an empty list DOES mean is that the site cannot be published yet — read it before you offer to publish anything, and read it before you offer to choose a hostname, because a business that already has one cannot have another.

operations.summary: Is this free web address available? Nothing is taken and nothing is held.
operations.description:
Ask whether a free web address is available. **This is the operation that makes you useful rather than decorative.** A client whose first six choices are gone is exactly who needs help, and you can only help if you can check: propose `colesbakery`, find it taken, check `colesbakerydublin` and `bakerybycole`, and come back with three that are actually free. A suggestion you have not checked is worse than no suggestion.

**Call it as often as you like.** It changes nothing, it holds nothing, and it costs nothing.

**But it is not a promise.** Two people can check the same name in the same second and both be told yes; whoever takes it first keeps it. So never tell your client a name IS theirs because you checked it — tell them it is free, and that taking it is what makes it theirs. If it goes while they are deciding, say so without ceremony — *that one went while you were deciding* — and offer the next one you checked.

**SAY THE WHOLE ADDRESS, ALWAYS.** `alice.1stc.site`, never `alice`. The answer carries it in full for exactly this reason, and a client who only ever heard the first word has not read the thing they are about to own for good.

**A refusal here is not always about availability, and the three lead three different places.** Somebody has it — try another name. It is one we keep — change the WORD, because every decoration of a kept word is kept too. It is not a valid address — fix the shape, and the rule is in the parameter. The sentence tells you which; say the right one, because it is what tells your client what to do next.

operations.summary: Take the free web address. This cannot be undone, changed, or swapped later.
operations.description:
Give your client's BUSINESS its free web address, permanently.

**IT IS THE BUSINESS'S ADDRESS, NOT THIS SITE'S**, and say it that way. One business holds one, for good, whatever it does with its sites afterwards — *"this site's address"* promises something narrower than what is actually being taken, and the pane beside this conversation says *your business's address* in the moment it asks them to confirm.

**Say what this is before you do it, not after.** In their words: this is the address on the van, on the card, in the search result. It is `alice.1stc.site` — the WHOLE thing, said in full, spelled out if there is any doubt — and it **cannot be changed afterwards**. Not by you, not by the form, not by us on request. A permanent name typed in a hurry is a permanent typo, so read it back to them exactly as it will be and get a clear yes to that string.

**Check first, then claim.** Not because the claim needs it — the claim decides on its own — but because being told "taken" is a better conversation than being refused after committing. And a claim that comes back taken anyway is the ordinary race, not a failure: *that one went while you were deciding*, and the next name you checked is one sentence away.

**One per business.** If they already have one, this refuses and names it; there is no second address and no way to trade one in.

**Say what it does NOT do.** It does not publish, it does not change the business's name, and the address does not go live until the site is published. What it DOES do is remove the thing that was stopping a publish: a site with no address cannot go live, because there would be nothing for anyone to type.

**If your client is not sure, let them not be sure.** There is no deadline and nothing is broken in the meantime. Reserving-by-claiming is exactly the mistake this operation makes unrecoverable.

groups.title: Reading the business's record
groups.description: What the business is called. Nothing here changes anything.

groups.title: Changing what the business is called
groups.description: Its own capability, and deliberately separate from reading: the record is the business's own identity to the product, and changing it is a decision rather than a lookup. It is also cheap and reversible — nothing is addressed by this name — which is why it is a text field and not a ceremony.

groups.title: Reading and checking public addresses
groups.description: Where your client's site can be reached, and whether a free web address they are considering is available. Nothing here takes anything, holds anything or changes anything — a check is a question, asked as many times as you like.

groups.title: Taking a public address
groups.description: Its own capability, and the most consequential thing on this surface. A free web address is global, first-come and **final**: one per BUSINESS, chosen once, never changed and never re-issued to anybody else. It is deliberately separate from checking, because checking is free and this is not — and separate from renaming the business, because that is a text field and this is a decision your client lives with.

sequences.name: Your client tells you the business name is wrong
sequences.note: Read it first so you can say what it is changing FROM, then rename, then read the effects back to them as offers. The site is not touched by any of this — if they want the site to follow, that is a site edit you make afterwards and they publish when they are ready.

sequences.name: Your client wants a free web address
sequences.note: Read first, because a business that already has one cannot have another and the whole conversation would be wasted. Then check — as many candidates as it takes, and you may check several before saying anything, so that what you offer is a short list of names that are actually free. Then, only once they have heard the whole address said back to them in full and understood that it is permanent — their business's address for good — claim it. If the claim comes back taken, that is the ordinary race and not a failure: say *that one went while you were deciding* and offer the next one you checked.

sequences.name: Your client asks why they cannot publish
sequences.note: An empty list is the answer. A site with no public address cannot be published, because there would be nothing for anyone to type — so the fix is a free web address here, or a domain they own, and either one is enough. Publishing itself is not something you do on this surface; the assistant beside their site does that.

absences.name: Changing what the site says
absences.note: There is nothing here that edits a site. The site's title is `config.businessName` and page copy is prose; both are site edits, made with the site's own operations, and both stay in the draft until your client publishes. That separation is the point of this surface, not a gap in it.

absences.name: Publishing
absences.note: Nothing here publishes. A rename publishes nothing and taking a hostname publishes nothing — publication has its own meaning and its own moment, and a settings change that pushed a draft live would release work your client never asked to release. What taking a hostname DOES do is remove the thing that was stopping a publish, and the publishing itself happens beside their site.

absences.name: Changing or releasing a hostname
absences.note: There is no operation that changes a hostname, swaps one, or gives one back — not a guarded one and not one we can perform on request. A hostname is chosen once and does not change, and nothing that has been issued is ever re-issued to anybody else. If it could be swapped freely, one business could walk through dozens of good names in an afternoon, and this is a first-come namespace that only ever gets smaller. Do not promise a change, do not imply one is coming, and do not offer to ask.

absences.name: A domain your client already owns
absences.note: Connecting a domain they bought elsewhere is real and is not built yet. Say that plainly if they ask: it is coming, it is not here, and a 1stc.site hostname is not a lesser substitute for it — a site can eventually have both.

absences.name: Choosing a hostname for them
absences.note: Nothing here mints, assigns or suggests-and-takes an address. You may propose as many names as you like and check every one of them, but the taking is your client's decision and the operation only ever does exactly what it was told. THIS HOLDS WHEN THEY ASK YOU TO DECIDE — *"just pick one"* is not consent to a particular name, and the answer to it is to say your favourite of the ones you checked and get a yes to that address, in full. A permanent public name chosen on somebody's behalf is the one mistake on this surface that cannot be corrected.

absences.name: Another business
absences.note: Every operation here is about the business this conversation is with. There is no way to name another one, and no way to find out what another account has called theirs.
